title: US Army Special Forces Recruitment 2026: Green Beret Path
metaDescription: US Army Special Forces recruitment 2026: 18X contract, SFAS selection, age and GT score requirements, Q Course length, and realistic pass rates explained.
headline: US Army Special Forces Recruitment 2026: How to Become a Green Beret

sections.title: Two routes into Special Forces
sections.content:
Civilians can enlist directly through the 18X Special Forces enlistment contract, which guarantees a slot at Special Forces Assessment and Selection (SFAS) but not acceptance into the force. Serving soldiers can also apply, usually from rank E-3 upward with command approval.

The 18X pipeline takes roughly two and a half to three years in total. It includes 22 weeks of Infantry training, three weeks of Airborne School, a preparation course, SFAS itself, and then the long Special Forces Qualification Course, known as the Q Course.

sections.title: Eligibility requirements
sections.content:
Civilian candidates must be US citizens, at least 20 years old by their ship date and not yet 32, with a high school diploma or GED. They need an ASVAB General Technical score of 110 or higher and eligibility for a Secret security clearance.

Serving soldiers generally must be 20 at SFAS, not older than 36 with a waiver, and hold a Defense Language Aptitude Battery score of 85 or higher. All candidates must meet Army height, weight and medical standards and volunteer for Airborne training.

sections.title: SFAS and the Q Course
sections.content:
SFAS lasts about three weeks, usually 19 to 24 days, at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. It tests physical endurance, land navigation, team events and psychological resilience, and selection rates are low: roughly 30 to 40 percent for 18X candidates and around 19 percent for prior-service transfers.

Selected candidates enter the Q Course, which lasts 18 to 28 months depending on specialty and language. Specialties include Weapons, Engineering, Medical and Communications, and language training is a core part of the course.

sections.title: Pay, bonus and honest odds
sections.content:
Reports put the standard 18X enlistment bonus for a six-year contract between $34,000 and $42,000 in 2026, though bonuses change with Army needs. Base pay follows rank and time in service, with special-duty and language pay on top.

Overall pipeline success is only about 10 to 15 percent, so most candidates do not finish as Green Berets. Those who do not make it are typically reassigned to conventional infantry units, which is why candidates should enlist only if they are willing to serve in the regular Army too.

faqs.q: What age do you need to join Army Special Forces?
faqs.a: Civilian 18X candidates must be at least 20 years old by their ship date to Infantry training and must not have reached their 32nd birthday by that date. Serving soldiers must generally be 20 at the start of SFAS and not older than 36, with waivers possible. Age rules sit alongside citizenship, education, fitness and clearance requirements.

faqs.q: What GT score is needed for Special Forces?
faqs.a: Candidates need an ASVAB General Technical score of 110 or higher, plus a Defense Language Aptitude Battery score of 85 or higher for most routes. The GT score is a hard screen, not a guideline: candidates below it cannot proceed to SFAS, even with strong fitness, so retaking the ASVAB to raise the GT score is often the first step.

faqs.q: How long is SFAS and the Q Course?
faqs.a: Special Forces Assessment and Selection lasts about three weeks, typically 19 to 24 days, covering physical tests, land navigation, team events and psychological evaluation. Selected candidates then enter the Qualification Course, lasting 18 to 28 months depending on specialty and language. The full civilian pipeline takes roughly two and a half to three years.

faqs.q: What happens if you fail SFAS?
faqs.a: Failing SFAS does not end Army service. Candidates who are not selected are typically reassigned to conventional infantry units to complete their enlistment. Overall pipeline success is only about 10 to 15 percent, so candidates should be honest about this risk before signing. Some may get another chance later as serving soldiers.
